III. 
Formal Sanctioning Support and Oversight of Projects Included in the 
Investment Plan 
 
Throughout the year, IT projects are subject to a formal governance process that includes a review 
and approval for all projects greater than $0.030 million.  Within IT, there is a team that reviews 
all IT projects before forwarding the project to the appropriate sanctioning authority for approval.  
Business Sponsored IT Investments up to $50 million that are classified as “Grow” will require 
both IT & Business approval. 
 
 Projects less than $10 million are approved by the US CIOs for their portfolios through a 
workflow approval process and under their delegations of authority.   
 Projects from $10 million to $25 million are approved by the Senior IT Leadership 
through a workflow approval process and under their delegations of authority.   
 Projects from $25 million to $50 million are approved by the Global CIO through a 
workflow approval process and under their delegation of authority. 
 Projects from $50 million to $203 million are approved by the New York and New England 
Executive Sanctioning Committees (“NYESC” and “NEESC”), under delegation of 
authority by the President, New York Jurisdiction and President, New England 
Jurisdiction.   In addition, these committees will also approve any projects less than this 
amount which are IT projects classified as Transform and any other Projects at its 
discretion without regard to whether such Projects exceed the $50 million threshold. 
 Projects which exceed the $203 million threshold must go to the Group Investment 
Committee for approval. 
 
IT projects are typically initially sanctioned for Requirements and Design work (also referred to 
as “Partial Sanction”) and then will return for Development and Implementation sanction (also 
referred to as “Sanction” or “Full Sanction”).  If project scope and costs are well understood (e.g., 
upgrades to hardware that do not necessitate requirements and design work or whose cost estimate 
can be reliably informed by similar previous installations), a project may proceed directly to 
“Sanction.”  In the event a project is forecast to exceed its sanction amount, a project must return 
to the appropriate Governance Committee for “Re-Sanction” consideration.  A “Closure” paper is 
prepared at the completion of a project detailing the financial and objective outcomes of the 
project.   
 
The Investment Plan includes all IT projects that progress from initial Feasibility & Analysis 
phases to ultimate closure to plant in service, as defined below, and supported by the formal 
sanctioning and governance process discussed above.  
 
 Feasibility & Analysis – A study conducted in cases where a significant level of analysis 
is required to better determine the direction or approach for a project.  Because such a study 
is likely to have a significant impact on IT resources and spend, the effort is treated as a 
project to be included in the Investment Plan. 
Exhibit ___ (ITDP-3R) 
Page 4 of 31


--- Page 358 ---
Page 4 of 12 
 
 Requirements & Design – This phase includes requirements definition and completion of 
analysis, confirmed project scope, agreed functional design, and technology solution to 
meet business and technical requirements, confirmed plan for Development and 
Implementation, and confirmed production handover, support strategy, and sourcing 
approach. 
 Development & Implementation – This phase includes development to the specified 
designs, testing, preparation for training, deployment of the solution to the business, and 
post-implementation support.   
 Project Closure – This phase closes the project, including capturing ongoing RTB costs, 
completing post implementation review and lessons learned, closing open actions and 
change requests, implementing a decommissioning plan for replaced technologies, and 
submitting a closure paper to the appropriate sanctioning committee.  
 
Cost estimates for projects that have completed the Requirements & Design stage with full scope 
and solution design generally have +/- 10% cost estimates.  Other projects at earlier stages, and 
the budgets for those projects, are less refined and more susceptible to changes in scope and budget.  
The projects in the Investment Plan are continuously reviewed for changes in assumptions, 
constraints, project delays, accelerations, and system operations, performance, safety, 
regulatory/compliance and customer driven needs that arise.  The sanctioning process allows a 
further evaluation of the total expected costs of a project at key points in the project’s lifecycle, 
including a view of how a given fiscal year’s spend on the project relates to the costs included in 
the Investment Plan as incorporated in the corporate budget.   
 
IV. 
Capital Plan Investments by Spending Categories 
 
The Company’s FY23 Plan is presented by portfolio category/spending rationale as shown below. 
 
A.  Group Functions  
Group Functions executes National Grid’s digital roadmaps, leveraging technology and 
reimagining processes in support of Finance, Enterprise Business Services, Human Resources, 
Legal, and Safety Health & Environmental, continuing to upgrade SOX related systems, and 
retiring outdated systems.   The 5 largest Investments within this portfolio are as follows: 
 
1. NG.com Refresh (INVP 6514US) – This investment is to refresh our externally facing web 
platform NG.com. NG.com provides the public face to National Grid's customers, 
communities and stakeholders. It offers the starting point for engagement with our 
organisation and key information to wider businesses who work with National Grid. 
 
2. SAP non-production landscapes (INVP 5607) - Procuring, setting up and configuring 
project environments is a critical path task for SAP related projects and initiatives. These 
activities can be time consuming and costly when done in isolation. To improve IT project 
implementation schedules, National Grid IT introduced a process to provide annual 
funding at the beginning of each fiscal year to procure and configure a set of project 
environments in support of all initiatives within the SAP portfolio for that fiscal 
year.  Appropriate costs will be associated with individual projects by issuing separate 
Exhibit ___ (ITDP-3R) 
Page 5 of 31


--- Page 359 ---
Page 5 of 12 
 
work orders for each project.  This method enables accurate cost treatment of the 
environments. 
 
3. My Hub 2.0 (INVP 5158) – The investment will move myHub to a standard configuration 
and reinforce it as a single source of workforce data.  The control environment will be 
strengthened through simplifying integrations and ensuring workforce data is aligned 
across the Company’s systems.  MyHub will improve efficiency in supporting our 
Operating Model by removing Joiners to Leavers complexity, improving user experience 
and process efficiency. It will unlock standard reporting and full workforce analytics 
capability and define the workforce master data model, ownership and governance. 
 
4. Lease Accounting Update (PowerPlan) (INVP 5497) - Powerplan is National Grid’s 
mission critical financial asset, project and tax system. This project will upgrade the 
application and all its underlying architecture to the latest version to bring National Grid 
back into support. The standalone Lease module also will be consolidated into the upgraded 
core Powerplan solution. 
 
5. FP&A Business Planning Modelling and Use cases (Global US) (INVP 6461USA) - This 
program of work will support overall Plan to Perform end to end process to deliver the 
Group Finance ambition to ensure flawless service and proactive, quality insights that 
drives performance and enhance forecasting and budgeting process.   The investment will 
provide planning and modelling tooling for group planning and budgeting, including 
financial and non-financial key drivers, automation of cost allocations and variance 
analysis reporting.   Data flows will be streamlined from source systems.    
 
B. United States Electric Business Unit 
IT supports the US Electric Distribution and Transmission businesses in modernizing key legacy 
operational systems while building capabilities that will effectively enable the energy transition.   
Through digital delivery, the Electric CIO organization provides greater efficiency and data driven 
insights into our workforce operations:  
 More automated and reliable grid controls systems  
 Capital programs and projects that support the growth of Distributed Energy Resources 
(DERs)  
 A growing market of prosumer electric customers 
 
Key projects within the Electric portfolio in FY23 include: 
 
1. Digital Warehouse (Track Me) (INVP 6388) - Validation and development work with a 
suite of Digital Products (i.e., ICU-Out, TrackMe, Digital Supervisor, etc.). Digital 
Warehouse will provide automation of inventory tracking, sophisticated demand 
forecasting and cross-shop visibility of warehousing.  The outcomes of this product will be 
reductions in obsolete materials, decreasing frequency of manual inventory inspections, 
avoiding double ordering, reduction in overall inventory size and reduction in schedule 
delays.

2. Digital Supervisor (SuperView) (INVP 6388) - Digital Supervisor Assistant will streamline 
and automate the processing of daily paperwork.  The system will work alongside On My 
Way (OMW).  SuperView will further enable barns and yards to go paperless and reduce 
time spent manually processing paper forms, manual input errors and improve compliance 
activities. 
 
3. ICU - Out (INVP 6291) - This product is part of the electric digital portfolio that will 
accelerate benefits to the electric business through digital transformation.  The product will 
provide an advanced customer outage solution that will analyze and integrate outage 
information from multiple systems and sources to generate a holistic view of an outage 
event. This is expected to reduce time and costs in restoring power outages through better 
data analytics that will enable us to better understand customer outage status / location, 
grid damage, along with having more advanced prediction of storm impacts. 
 
Currently we rely primarily on customers calling to report outages to determine where 
outages are.  This causes inefficiencies because not all customers call within a timely period 
of the outage occurring. 
 
Opportunities available through digitization include: 
 Improved data quality 
 Improved outage area predictions 
 Improved or eliminated manual processes 
 Improved visibility into field conditions 
 Improved customer communications 
 
4. Future Now (INVP 6076) – Work planning in the Electric Business Unit (EBU) is a manual 
process involving multiple systems which are not fully integrated.  This investment will 
complete the development and roll out of FutureNow optimization capabilities to the 
Transmission Business enabling the EBU to maximize strategic objectives against budget 
and resources. 
 
5. Vegetation. Management Optimization (VMO) (INVP 6073) - This digital project seeks to 
maximize the value of National Grid’s vegetation management programs. The product 
aims to provide the capability to plan tree pruning activities based on condition, using 
advanced analytics and other available technologies, instead of pruning on fixed time 
cycles.  It will assess technologies to maximize value during the execution of the pruning 
activities. The product also seeks opportunities to drive value in the hazard tree program 
management, in terms of both planning and execution.  Features will include Sub-Circuit 
pruning and improved reliability. 
 
6. Retail Settlement (INVP 5891E) - Planning and development work to implement a new 
Retail Settlement system for FY24.  The company has recently implemented a new 
Wholesale Settlement solution, replacing two end of life systems which were no longer 
supportable due to out dated components, infrastructure and application code. This 
investment will allow for consolidation with the new Wholesale Settlement system released 
in FY22.

E. Infrastructure and Operations (“I&O”) 
The I&O area supports National Grid’s internal IT Architecture covering Cloud and Hosting, 
Critical Network Infrastructure, Networks, End User Experience and Operations.  I&O is focused 
on reducing National Grid’s technical debt through cost effective, modernized IT infrastructure 
enabling cloud capabilities that meet our risk profile.  The organization enables a connected, 
seamless enterprise that is flexible, secure, reliable and scalable while maintaining acceptable 
levels of technical debt and risk.  Key I&O programs include: 
 
1. I&O US End User Experience FY23 (INVP 6487) - End users need to be more engaged, 
agile, secure, and therefore productive and efficient through the technologies that they 
interact with daily. The investment will focus on improving the technology experience for 
our end users, employees, contractors and partners.  Initiatives include:  
 Enhanced developer capabilities with fully managed MAC solution. Devices 
(laptops/desktops) refreshed as per policy. 
 Perpetual Windows, Browser & Office Currency (Windows as a Service). Remote 
PC/MAC provisioning and configuration.  
 Expanded replacement of aging Video Conferencing equipment with MS Team 
compatible equipment providing frictionless, simplified and improved end user 
experience.   
 Device & Data Access (DDA) - Provide our colleagues with appropriate devices 
which enable them to securely access applications and data. 
 Real Time Collaboration (RTC) - Enable high quality synchronous digital 
interactions between people with very low latency. 
 Content Collaboration (CC) - Deliver asynchronous, highly available applications 
which allow colleagues to co-create business workflows and documents. 
 Support Assurance - Deliver a multi-channel, cost-effective and digital suite of 
provisioning, support and knowledge experiences. 
 Digital Adoption and Change (DA&CM) - Prepare and enable the business to 
efficiently adopt our digital productivity and collaboration experiences.

delivery enabled through simplified, platform agnostic provisioning and increased 
automation of workloads.

(Container as a Service CaaS).   
 Technical debt reduction – decommission of EoSL devices and continued migration

standardizing technology.   
 Private Cloud Platforms - An automated, secure and standardized application 
platform similar to Public Cloud but within the dedicated hosting environment for 
National Grid.    
 Public Cloud Platforms - Public Cloud enabled for National Grid specific 
business/security requirements.    
 Cloud Containers - Optimize application utilization and enable workload mobility.    
 Global Access Management - Global AD for secure access to entire corporate 
estate.

 Improved stability and reduced Mean Time to Resolve for eligible applications.

F. Security 
The Security function protects our people, premises, and digital systems with the objective of 
maintaining trust in National Grid services, focusing on: 
 
Reduction in likelihood and impact of security incidents 
 
Compliance with relevant laws, standards and regulations (e.g., NERC, PCI DSS, GDPR, 
NIS-R) 
 
Improved user experience and standard of security practices across National Grid 
 
The Security function aims to reduce the likelihood and impact of physical and cyber security 
incidents affecting National Grid. It does this by championing security best practices, technology 
and promoting a security-awareness culture.  
 
1. Physical Security (INVP 3617) – This project will deliver improvements to security at 
physical locations by upgrading monitoring systems and supporting infrastructure to 
maintain regulatory compliance for monitoring and safety of our people and premises.  The 
project will replace out of support and warranty field units where failure may result in 
extended replacement lead times or inability to obtain like-for-like replacements.  It will 
also improve the quality of monitoring with high quality video capture and detection 
systems. 
 
2. Cyber Operational Technology (INVP 5933) – This project will deliver improvements to 
National Grid's network resilience and defense in depth capabilities to facilitate our ability 
Exhibit ___ (ITDP-3R) 
Page 12 of 31


--- Page 366 ---
Page 12 of 12 
 
to identify cyber risks and threats, protect and detect against malicious cyber activity and 
effectively respond to and recover from cyber incidents at operational sites.  
 
3. Vulnerability Management (INVP 6417US) – This project will deliver improvements to 
National Grid’s penetration testing, vulnerability scanning and web application scanning 
capabilities that identify vulnerabilities and facilitate prioritization for remediation based 
on risk.  
 
4. Network Security (INVP 6526US) This project will deliver improvements that reduce the 
likelihood of cyber incidents related to distributed denial of service attacks, and protect 
against and enable detection of network traffic related to malware, which can propagate 
through the network if traffic is not monitored or alerted upon.  
 
5. Platform Security (INVP 6480US) – This project will deliver improvements that reduce 
the likelihood of cyber incidents related to malware and exploitation of insecure system 
configurations, identify high value hardening activities, assess impact on operational 
stability and environments, test and implement system hardening and improve mobile 
threat defense. 
 
6. Security Orchestration Automation and Response (INVP 
6540US) - This project will 
deliver improvements to response and recovery capability, reduce the overall impact 
duration of an incident and implement advanced threat detection capabilities that factor 
changes to the threat landscape.  
 
7. Identity and Access Management (INVP 5870) - This project will deliver improvements 
that reduce the likelihood of cyber incidents relating to unauthorized access or misuse of 
access privileges, and privileges on critical applications.  
 
V. 
Conclusion 
 
Consistent with Section IV.10.5 of the Joint Proposal for cases 20-E-0380 and 20-G-0381 and 
Section IV.6.5 for Cases 19-G-0309 and 19-G-0310, the Company will provide quarterly variance 
reports within 60 days after the end of each Fiscal Year quarter.  The reports will address the status 
of IT programs and budgets.  On a semi-annual basis, the Company will also meet with Department 
of Public Service Staff to discuss budget and actual spending to date and discuss project status.

Fiscal Year 2024 Information Technology 
Capital Investment Plan 
I.
Introduction
Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation (Niagara Mohawk), The Brooklyn Union Gas Company 
(KEDNY), and KeySpan Gas East Corporation (KEDLI) (together “National Grid” or the 
“Companies”) submits its Information Technology (“IT”) Capital Investment Plan (the 
“Investment Plan”) for fiscal year 2024 (“FY24 Plan”).1  This submission is in compliance with 
Section IV.6.5 of the Joint Proposal adopted by the New York Public Service Commission (“PSC” 
or the “Commission”) January 20, 2022 in Cases 20-E-0380 and 20-G-0381, and Section IV.10.5 
of the Joint Proposal adopted by the Commission August 12, 2021 in Cases 19-G-0309 and 19-G-
0310.2 
IT capital projects and investments that are shared investments across National Grid’s operating 
companies are implemented and owned by National Grid USA Service Company, Inc. (“Service 
Company”) and allocated to the benefiting US operating companies, including Niagara Mohawk, 
KEDNY and KEDLI in the form of an annual rent expense once the investments are in-service.  
The rent expense includes a return on the capital investment plus depreciation expense.   
The FY24 Plan is made up of in-flight projects that will require capital spending to complete as 
well as projects that will be sanctioned and begin to incur capital charges during the fiscal year. 
In total, the FY24 Plan reflects Service Company capital expenditures of $295.625 million across 
the US operating companies.  Of this amount, approximately $290.563 million is for projects that 
benefit and, therefore, are chargeable to Niagara Mohawk, $225.530 million to KEDNY and 
$261.730 million to KEDLI.3  The FY24 Plan provided in Attachment 1 includes a list of projects, 
forecast in-service dates, and the allocators used to determine the rent expense for the operating 
companies that will benefit from each project, along with FY24 Service Company IT capital costs 
and the full Service Company project spend expected for each investment.   
National Grid’s IT organization continuously reviews the Investment Plan relative to current 
business requirements, risks and information.  The FY24 Plan assumes that large-scale economic, 
political, and environmental events will not significantly impact the Capital Investment Plan or 
1 FY24 is from April 1, 2023 through March 31, 2024.

II.
Development of the Capital Plan
National Grid engages in an iterative process that involves collaboration with Jurisdictional 
representatives and the functional business areas (e.g., Operations, Customer and Digital, Network 
Strategy, and Finance and Shared Services) to identify the investments of highest priority for 
inclusion in the Capital Investment Plan.  This process aligns with the corporate budgeting process 
and strategic portfolio reviews.  
The development of the IT FY24 Plan was based on an assessment and analysis of current and 
proposed programs aligned to the Company’s IT strategic focus - build and maintain the 
foundation, drive new capabilities, and enable cost savings.  We reviewed each program and 
balanced funding across focus areas to optimize investments and drive value.  The FY24 Plan 
focuses on the following: 
•
Fulfilling regulatory and legal mandates
•
Reducing cyber and operational risk
•
Driving standardization and modernization
•
Building tools and platforms to empower our people
•
Safeguarding critical business applications
•
Building new capabilities for improved business performance
•
Implementing cost efficiencies and saving programs to achieve year-over-year run-the-
business (“RTB”) cost reductions
In building the IT FY24 Plan, National Grid first identified the amount of work remaining and the 
delivery timeline for in-flight, multi-year investments.  Next, new investments to address 
compliance with a legal or regulatory requirement/mandate or an open corporate risk were added 
to the Plan.  Third, investments that focused on IT infrastructure – primarily investments to 
upgrade/replace/add functionality that would create reliability in systems and fix foundational 
capabilities necessary for operations and/or future aspirations of the business (including ensuring 
digital security) were included.  Finally, the IT team worked closely with the Jurisdiction and 
business executive sponsors to focus on their top project requests.   
After this analysis, IT distributed a draft Investment Plan to business functions, Jurisdictional 
representatives, and other key stakeholders for feedback and held review sessions on the proposed 
plan.  A final Investment Plan review occurs each fiscal year with the Jurisdictional Presidents, 
Jurisdictional delegates, and functional executives.  Upon the review and approval of the 
Investment Plan by the Jurisdictional Presidents and functional executives, the consolidated 
financial information from the Plan, by jurisdiction and company, is incorporated with the IT 
O&M requirements into the IT budget.  The IT budget is then reviewed and approved by the New 
York Chief Information Officer (“CIO”), Global CIO, and Corporate Finance, and is incorporated 
into a consolidated National Grid USA budget for approval by the National Grid plc Board.

III.
Formal Sanctioning Support and Oversight of Projects Included in the
Investment Plan
Throughout the year, IT projects are subject to a formal governance process that includes a review 
and approval for all projects greater than $0.030 million.  Within IT, there is a team that reviews 
all IT projects before forwarding the project to the appropriate sanctioning authority for approval.  
Business Sponsored IT Investments up to $50 million that are classified as “Grow” will require 
both IT & Business approval. 
•
Projects less than $10 million are approved by the CIOs for their portfolios through a
workflow approval process and under their delegations of authority.
•
Projects from $10 million to $25 million are approved by the Senior IT Leadership
through a workflow approval process and under their delegations of authority.
•
Projects from $25 million to $50 million are approved by the Global CIO through a
workflow approval process and under their delegation of authority.
•
Projects from $50 million to $203 million are approved by the New York and New England
Executive Sanctioning Committees (“NYESC” and “NEESC”), under delegation of
authority by the President, New York Jurisdiction and President, New England
Jurisdiction.   In addition, these committees will also approve any projects less than this
amount which are IT projects classified as Transform and any other Projects at its
discretion without regard to whether such Projects exceed the $50 million threshold.
•
Projects which exceed the $203 million threshold must go to the Group Investment
Committee for approval.
IT projects are typically initially sanctioned for Requirements and Design work (also referred to 
as “Partial Sanction”) and then will return for Development and Implementation sanction (also 
referred to as “Sanction” or “Full Sanction”).  If project scope and costs are well understood (e.g., 
upgrades to hardware that do not necessitate requirements and design work or whose cost estimate 
can be reliably informed by similar previous installations), a project may proceed directly to 
“Sanction.”  In the event a project is forecast to exceed its sanction amount, a project must return 
to the appropriate Governance Committee for “Re-Sanction” consideration.  A “Closure” paper is 
prepared at the completion of a project detailing the financial and objective outcomes of the 
project.   
The Investment Plan includes all IT projects that progress from initial Feasibility & Analysis 
phases to ultimate closure to plant in service, as defined below, and supported by the formal 
sanctioning and governance process discussed above.  
•
Feasibility & Analysis – A study conducted in cases where a significant level of analysis
is required to better determine the direction or approach for a project.  Because such a study
is likely to have a significant impact on IT resources and spend, the effort is treated as a
project to be included in the Investment Plan.
Exhibit ___ (ITDP-3R) 
Page 20 of 31


--- Page 374 ---
Page 4 of 12 
•
Requirements & Design – This phase includes requirements definition and completion of
analysis, confirmed project scope, agreed functional design, and technology solution to
meet business and technical requirements, confirmed plan for Development and
Implementation, and confirmed production handover, support strategy, and sourcing
approach.
•
Development & Implementation – This phase includes development to the specified
designs, testing, preparation for training, deployment of the solution to the business, and
post-implementation support.
•
Project Closure – This phase closes the project, including capturing ongoing RTB costs,
completing post implementation review and lessons learned, closing open actions and
change requests, implementing a decommissioning plan for replaced technologies, and
submitting a closure paper to the appropriate sanctioning committee.
Cost estimates for projects that have completed the Requirements & Design stage with full scope 
and solution design generally have +/- 10% cost estimates.  Other projects at earlier stages, and 
the budgets for those projects, are less refined and more susceptible to changes in scope and budget.  
The projects in the Investment Plan are continuously reviewed for changes in assumptions, 
constraints, project delays, accelerations, and system operations, performance, safety, 
regulatory/compliance and customer driven needs that arise.  The sanctioning process allows a 
further evaluation of the total expected costs of a project at key points in the project’s lifecycle, 
including a view of how a given fiscal year’s spend on the project relates to the costs included in 
the Investment Plan as incorporated in the corporate budget.

of project environments in support of all initiatives within the SAP portfolio for that
fiscal year.  Appropriate costs will be associated with individual projects by issuing
separate work orders for each project.  This method enables accurate cost treatment of the
environments.

F. Security 
The Security function protects our people, premises, and digital systems with the objective of 
maintaining trust in National Grid services, focusing on: 
• Reduction in likelihood and impact of security incidents 
• Compliance with relevant laws, standards and regulations (e.g., NERC, PCI DSS, GDPR, 
NIS-R) 
• Improved user experience and standard of security practices across National Grid 
 
The Security function aims to reduce the likelihood and impact of physical and cyber security 
incidents affecting National Grid. It does this by championing security best practices, technology 
and promoting a security-awareness culture.

Consistent with Section IV.10.5 of the Joint Proposal for cases 20-E-0380 and 20-G-0381 and 
Section IV.6.5 for Cases 19-G-0309 and 19-G-0310, the Company will provide quarterly variance 
reports within 60 days after the end of each Fiscal Year quarter.  The reports will address the status 
of IT programs and budgets.  On a semi-annual basis, the Company will also meet with Department 
of Public Service Staff to discuss budget and actual spending to date and discuss project status.

Comprehensive Management and

24 
Chapter 2: Information Systems 
Recommendation: 12 (page 40) 
The Utilities should improve quarterly variance reports for Information Systems projects.  
Implementation Leads  
Executive Sponsor: 
Erik Barthel – NY CIO  
Team Lead(s): 
Daniel J. DeMauro, Jr. – Director, IT Regulatory 
Jim Reynolds – Director, IT Finance 
Caitlin Davidson – Director, US IT PMO 
Implementation Priority: High 
Recommendation Accepted: Yes (with modification) 
Current Status: Implemented 
Background Information: 
As part of its rate plan in Cases 17-E-0238 and 17-G-0239, NMPC provides information to Staff 
and the Commission about IT project selection and budgeting.  Prior to each of its rate years, 
NMPC files with the Commission its IT Capital Investment Plan for the upcoming rate year, 
including the overall IT investment plan for that year, the process for developing the plan, and 
identification of the proposed IT projects and their estimated costs.  NMPC also files quarterly 
variance reports to address the status of the Service Company IT programs/projects and budgets. 
The variance reports include (i) a narrative explaining overall IT investment plan approach; (ii) a 
description of defined program categories (e.g., Regulatory, Legal and Compliance Mandates; 
Business Programs and Projects; Technology/Infrastructure Foundation and Reliability) that form 
the spending rationale for IT projects; (iii) detail on budgets and actual spending for each of the 
program categories, and for the top ten projects by budget within the program categories; (iv) 
explanations of variances between budgets and actual spending; (v) identification of allocations to 
NMPC; and (vi) a report on budget exceptions by program category and top ten projects based on 
allocations to NMPC.  In the report for the last quarter of each Rate Year, NMPC also includes (i) 
an explanation of any cost or timeline differences exceeding ten percent for projects completed; 
(ii) the latest partial, full, re-sanction or closure paper for any projects exceeding $1 million that
were authorized during the previous rate year; and (iii) performance on the IT capital cost
incentive.  NMPC also meets with Staff on a semi-annual basis to (i) discuss proposed projects for
the next six months; (ii) provide an update on the status of in-flight projects; (iii) discuss proposed
projects for the next six months; and (iv) review quarterly filings.  The Audit Report states (at 34)
that the information currently provided by NMPC is generally adequate but could benefit from
additional detail.
Exhibit ___ (ITDP-4R) 
Page 2 of 4


--- Page 388 ---
25 
At present, KEDNY and KEDLI do not have an IT reporting requirement in their current rate plan, 
but Staff filed testimony in their ongoing rate proceedings (Cases 19-G-0309 and 19-G-0310) (the 
“2019 KEDNY and KEDLI Rate Cases”) recommending that KEDNY and KEDLI adopt similar 
reporting requirements as NMPC and meet with Staff on a semi-annual basis.   
Most recently, on November 25, 2020, Staff filed testimony in NMPC’s current rate proceeding 
(Cases 20-E-0380 and 20-G-0381) (the “2020 NMPC Rate Case”) stating that the IT reporting 
requirements currently in effect for NMPC (as described above) require significant efforts from 
both NMPC to develop the reports and from Staff to review the reports.  At the same time, Staff 
testified that the IT reporting requirements do not necessarily provide the information in a format 
that permits easy monitoring and understanding of any individual IT project’s progress or enables 
full comprehension of the entire IT portfolio.  Therefore, Staff recommends collaborating with 
NMPC to develop streamlined and improved IT reporting requirements to enable easier monitoring 
of project progress in terms of schedule, scope, and budget.2 
Proposal to Implement Recommendation: 
KEDNY and KEDLI will implement IT reporting requirements that are ultimately adopted by the 
Commission in the 2019 KEDNY and KEDLI Rate Cases.  At the same time, the NY Operating 
Companies believe that collaboration with Staff is necessary to streamline the IT reporting process 
to provide benefits to National Grid and Staff, as recognized by the Staff Information Technology 
Panel in the 2020 NMPC Rate Case.  Therefore, the NY Operating Companies propose to meet 
with Staff within 120 days of the Commission’s order in the 2019 KEDNY and KEDLI Rate Cases 
to adopt an IT reporting framework that provides Staff with greater transparency into National 
Grid’s IT investment, sanctioning, budgeting, and approval process without creating an undue 
burden on the NY Operating Companies to compile the information and on Staff to review the 
information.   
Schedule: 
KEDNY and KEDLI will implement the new reporting consistent with the timelines adopted by 
the Commission in the 2019 KEDNY and KEDLI Rate Cases to be followed by a collaborative 
meeting with Staff within 120 days of that order.  At that meeting, the NY Operating Companies 
and Staff will develop a framework for IT reporting that can be utilized by the NY Operating 
Companies to address both the Audit Report recommendation as well as any obligations 
established in rate plans in a manner that aligns reporting across the NY Operating Companies.   
Summary of Cost/Benefit and Risk Analysis: 
Extending the current NMPC reporting requirements to KEDNY and KEDLI will require a 
significant amount of incremental information and documentation across the NY Operating 
Companies.  An incremental full time equivalent will be needed to compile this reporting on an 
ongoing basis.  The expectation is that National Grid and Staff can meet to discuss an enhanced 
2 See Cases 20-E-0380 and 20-E-3081, Staff Information Technology Panel’s testimony at 73-74.

Benefits are qualitative in nature and include improved visibility to variances and further

The deliverable to demonstrate that the recommendation has been implemented is submission to

Response: 
1.
a.
The IT&D Security function assesses risks that each physical security investment 
seeks to address and prioritizes them accordingly.  This risk-based approach is used to 
determine which sites are worked on and considers the following factors: 

Break-Fix – When an asset used to secure a physical location fails and the
Company’s ability to secure a site is compromised, break-fix work provides
temporary compensating controls to be implemented until longer-term solutions
can be completed to replace the failed asset with a like-for-like asset.  Break-Fix is
completed on an on-going and as-needed basis and takes funding priority.

The Company’s knowledge and management of assets – The Company
manages the lifecycle of assets used to secure sites and maintains an inventory of
asset age, vendor, make, model, warranty, and support.  A campaign of
replacements based on asset lifecycle proactively reduces break-fix work and
predicts which assets should be replaced ahead of failure.  It is based on whether
an asset is no longer supported, is discontinued, or is no longer as effective as
current solutions are.

Changes to physical site classification and physical security requirements –
The Company reviews physical sites on an on-going basis to assess site criticality
and vulnerability.  Changes to site criticality also change physical security needs
based on updated site classifications of low, medium, or high.

Site specific reports and required improvements – The Company assesses sites
on a proactive basis to identify gaps in physical security.  When gaps are
identified, they are prioritized for investment.  On a reactive basis, after a physical
security breach has occurred, a post-incident assessment is completed to
understand what controls are required to mitigate future events from occurring.
Those controls are prioritized for investment.
b.
The method and information used to determine which physical security threats and
vulnerabilities are prioritized and addressed is driven by the risk-based approach
described in the response to Question 1, as well as:

Site Criticality

Annual vulnerability assessments conducted at all critical facilities

Dedicated threat intelligence teams continuously monitor and assess the threat
landscape. (tactics, techniques, procedures (“TTPs”))

Collaboration and participation in a broad range of information sharing groups,
including with other utilities.  Information sharing groups include:

Electrical Information Sharing and Analysis Center (“E-ISAC”)

Downstream Natural Gas Information Sharing and Analysis Center (“DNG-
ISAC”)

Homeland Security Information Network (“HSIN”)

Energy Sector Analyst Roundtable (“ESAR”)

International Association of Law Enforcement Intelligence Analysts
(“IALEIA”)


Edison Electric Institute (“EEI”)

American Gas Association (“AGA”)

Interstate Natural Gas Association of America (“INGAA”)






customers.

Physical Security program investment occur at the end of a given fiscal year.

Long-term reduction of break-fix work by proactively replacing and upgrading

Leveraging internal resources when possible.

Securing and protecting the assets that are essential to the Company’s ability to
provide safe and reliable service to customers.


investments required to upgrade and maintain the supporting IT infrastructure that

2.
The following alternatives have been considered for the physical security program: 
a.
Do Nothing and replace through break-fix only – Not Accepted - While the 
existing physical security capabilities are functional, they do not feature capabilities 
on the market today, constraining the effectiveness of capabilities. A break-fix 
approach does not bring capabilities to current standards because it is like-for-like to 
ensure compatibility.  
b.
Accelerate proactive replacement program – Not Accepted – The current 
proactive replacement program has considered the useful life of existing assets, the 
useful life of replaced assets, internal resource availability for IT and Business 
Exhibit ___ (ITDP-5R) 
Page 10 of 11

Form 103
stakeholders to support on-going break-fix requirements, upgrades required due to 
site classification changes, regulatory changes, and site availability when determining 
the budget and in-scope sites. Acceleration of the proactive replacement campaign 
would require increased resources to deliver and increased funding to achieve. 
c.
Prioritize site-specific break-fix, proactive replacement of end-of-life assets, and
site by site physical security requirements – Accepted – The Company’s proposal
for funding considers the different aspects of the physical security program and the

to the regulatory requirements. This proposal enables the Company to ramp up or
down the different aspects of the program to address any immediate needs and
balance future needs for remediation or upgrade.
